metadata.narrative: I’m on a hospital nursing DEI council that has to recommend a three-year plan with limited money. Our chief nursing officer wants something that helps recruitment and retention, not just a one-time training. What should we prioritize across nursing school pipeline partnerships, hiring and promotion practices, reporting systems for racism, leadership accountability, and curriculum/continuing education? How should we think about tradeoffs, what outcomes should we measure, and what mistakes would make the plan feel performative to nurses of color?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A three-year DEI plan for a nursing council should function as a workforce-retention strategy built on interlocking systems rather than a single event, because isolated training sessions rarely change outcomes on their own.

Evidence from health systems that have tried to operationalize DEI shows the concept easily gets "co-opted and used solely for public relations and sloganeering" unless paired with structural changes such as pipeline partnerships, internships, and employee resource groups.
One hospital reported reaching 83% diverse nursing staff through sustained HBCU partnerships, internship pipelines, and Business Resource Groups rather than through a training mandate.

A genuinely sustained model comes from Carle Health, funded through the National Commission to Address Racism in Nursing, which paired a one-hour kickoff with 20 weeks of ongoing microlearning cascaded through frontline leaders specifically to avoid a one-and-done format.

On the pipeline side, the HRSA Nursing Workforce Diversity program's shift to holistic admissions found that 72% of participating schools increased applicant diversity with no decline in academic outcomes, showing pipeline investment need not lower standards.

A three-year HRSA-funded case study showed pipeline work needs dedicated staffing to succeed: hiring one retention specialist to track at-risk students by race and ethnicity, pair them with mentors, and build partnerships with feeder high schools produced measurable graduation and licensure gains within the grant period.

Given limited money, a council should fund one dedicated pipeline/retention coordinator role and two or three deep, staffed partnerships rather than spreading thin sponsorships across many institutions.

On hiring and promotion, underrepresented minority nurses receive less mentorship and sponsorship, are less often offered central or visible assignments, and report added pressure to "prove ability" compared with white peers, all of which slow advancement even at equal performance.

Because these barriers operate through informal sponsorship networks rather than overt exclusion, plans focused only on applicant-pool diversity without auditing who gets mentored and promoted will miss the actual mechanism driving disparities.

An organizational commitment to diversity should explicitly not mean lowering qualification standards, since credibility depends on advancement being seen as earned, but it does require building structured mentorship pipelines into management roles.

Reporting systems need redesign, not just existence: survey data show only 23% of nurses who experienced racism filed a formal report, most instead confiding in peers because they distrusted the process.

Nurses avoid HR and administration because they fear being blamed or retaliated against for reporting, a fear repeatedly raised by practitioners describing why formal systems fail even when they technically exist.

A national commission survey found that when nurses did report racism, only four in ten were satisfied with the response, and Black nurses were most likely to experience racism from a supervisor or leader specifically, meaning reporting systems need protections against manager retaliation and independent review outside the immediate chain of command.

Leadership accountability connects all the other pillars: research on "consequential accountability," meaning DEI progress is built into leaders' own performance evaluations, found organizations using it accelerated racial parity in leadership benches by roughly six years, while most organizations claiming to hold leaders accountable never tie DEI metrics to performance reviews.

A nursing commission on racism argued change "starts at the top" and that leaders must be accountable for their own actions and dismantle policies letting racist behavior by leaders go unaddressed, which matters given that leaders were a common source of racism reported by nurses.

Curriculum and continuing education should move past generic cultural-competence modules toward specific content, since nursing curricula have been criticized for a "dominance of whiteness" that omits pioneers like Mary Seacole and Mary Eliza Mahoney and under-prepares nurses to recognize symptoms across skin tones, a gap tied by one inquest to a patient death from an unrecognized sickle cell crisis.

Continuing education should be an ongoing cadence, such as recurring microlearning reinforced by frontline leaders, rather than an annual all-staff seminar, since that format sustains behavior change instead of delivering a single dose of awareness.
On tradeoffs with limited money, the council should sequence investment across the three years.
Year one should fund accountability infrastructure and redesign the reporting and anti-retaliation system, because these are prerequisites that make every later investment credible.
Year two should add the pipeline/retention coordinator role and mentorship-sponsorship structures for promotion.
Year three should scale continuing education into recurring microlearning and expand pipeline partnerships based on what earlier years show is working.

This sequencing reflects that accountability and trustworthy reporting are inexpensive relative to large training rollouts or grant-funded pipeline programs, yet they determine whether staff believe later, costlier investments are genuine.

For outcomes, the council should track nurse-of-color-specific turnover and retention rather than aggregate figures, since national nurse turnover already costs $28,400 to $51,700 per RN and $3.6 to $6.5 million per hospital annually, making retention gains among nurses of color financially material.

Workforce engagement data show employees with the lowest perception of DEI value are 4.3 to 4.6 times less likely to intend to stay three years, so the council should add a recurring DEI-perception pulse survey alongside exit interviews, promotion-rate-by-race tracking, and the share of racism reports resulting in documented action.
Finally, the plan will feel performative to nurses of color if it announces goals without funding the coordinator roles or protected reporting channels needed to reach them.

It will also feel performative if leadership accountability is asserted rhetorically without being written into performance reviews, if a single training event is treated as sufficient, or if reporting and promotion data are collected but never shared back with staff to show whether anything changed.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

output.text:
A three-year DEI plan for a nursing council should function as a workforce-retention strategy built on interlocking systems rather than a single event, because nurses of color and hospital leaders alike agree that isolated training sessions rarely change outcomes.
Evidence from health systems that have tried to operationalize DEI shows the concept easily gets "co-opted and used solely for public relations and sloganeering" unless it is paired with structural changes such as pipeline partnerships, internships, and employee resource groups that produce measurable diversity gains, as one hospital reported reaching 83% diverse nursing staff through sustained HBCU partnerships rather than a training mandate.
Genuinely sustained programs look like Carle Health's model, funded through the National Commission to Address Racism in Nursing, which paired a one-hour kickoff with 20 weeks of ongoing microlearning cascaded through frontline leaders specifically to avoid the one-and-done format your CNO is worried about.

On the pipeline side, the HRSA Nursing Workforce Diversity program's shift to holistic admissions found that 72% of participating schools increased diversity in their applicant pools with no decline in academic outcomes, showing that pipeline investment does not require lowering standards.
A three-year HRSA-funded case study at a school of nursing demonstrated that pipeline work needs dedicated staffing to succeed, since hiring a single retention specialist to track at-risk students by race and ethnicity, pair them with mentors, and build sustainable partnerships with local high schools produced concrete graduation and licensure gains within the grant period.
Given limited money, a council should prioritize funding one dedicated pipeline/retention coordinator role and two or three deep partnerships with local high schools or community colleges rather than spreading thin sponsorships across many institutions, since concentrated, staffed relationships appear to outperform diffuse ones.

On hiring and promotion, the structural barriers facing nurses of color are well documented: underrepresented minority nurses receive less mentorship and sponsorship, are less often offered central or visible assignments, and report added pressure to "prove ability" compared with white peers, all of which slow advancement even when performance is equal.
Because these barriers operate through informal sponsorship networks rather than overt exclusion, plans that focus only on job-posting language or applicant-pool diversity without also auditing who gets mentored, tapped for stretch assignments, and promoted into charge or management roles will miss the mechanism actually driving disparities.
An organizational commitment to diversity should explicitly not mean lowering qualification standards, since credibility with the broader nursing staff depends on advancement being seen as earned, but it does require actively building structured mentorship and sponsorship pipelines into management roles.

Reporting systems for racism need redesign, not just existence, because survey data show only 23% of nurses who experienced racism filed a formal report, most describing distrust that anything would be done, and instead confiding in peers instead of using official channels.
Nurses frequently avoid HR, administration, and even unions because they fear being blamed or retaliated against for reporting, a fear repeatedly raised by practitioners describing why formal systems fail even when they technically exist.
A national survey further found that when nurses did report racism, only four in ten were satisfied with the institutional response, and Black nurses were most likely of any group to experience racism from a supervisor or leader specifically, meaning reporting systems must include protections against manager retaliation and independent review outside the immediate chain of command.

Leadership accountability is the mechanism that connects all the other pillars, since research on "consequential accountability"—integrating DEI progress into leaders' own performance evaluations—found organizations using it accelerated racial parity in leadership benches by roughly six years compared with those that did not, while most organizations claiming to hold leaders accountable never actually tie DEI metrics to performance reviews.
A nursing-specific commission on racism explicitly argued change "starts at the top," warning that leaders must be accountable for their own actions and dismantle policies that let racist behavior by leaders go unaddressed, which matters given that survey data showed leaders were the most common source of racism reported by Black nurses.

Curriculum and continuing education should move past generic cultural-competence modules toward specific content, since nursing curricula have been criticized for a "dominance of whiteness" that omits pioneers like Mary Seacole and Mary Eliza Mahoney and under-prepares nurses to recognize symptoms across skin tones, a gap tied by one inquest to a patient death from an unrecognized sickle cell crisis.
Continuing education should be structured as an ongoing cadence, such as brief recurring microlearning modules reinforced by frontline leaders, rather than an annual all-staff seminar, since that format was specifically designed to sustain behavior change over time rather than deliver a single dose of awareness.

On tradeoffs with limited money, the council should sequence investment: year one should fund the accountability infrastructure (tying DEI metrics into leader performance reviews and redesigning the reporting/anti-retaliation system) because those are prerequisites that make every other investment credible; year two should add the dedicated pipeline/retention coordinator role and mentorship-sponsorship structures for promotion; year three should scale continuing education into recurring microlearning and expand pipeline partnerships based on what year one and two data show is working.
This sequencing reflects that accountability and trustworthy reporting are inexpensive relative to large-scale training rollouts or grant-funded pipeline programs, yet they determine whether staff believe later, costlier investments are genuine.
